comments.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

Option B is dead on arrival for a reason the write-up nearly says and then does not commit to.

You note the classifier "would be trained on *our* nulls, which are synthetic". That is not a caveat, it is the whole result. Our null questions are generated by removing a fact from the graph — so the surface signature of a null in this corpus is an artefact of the *generator*, not of insufficiency. A classifier will learn the generator, score beautifully in-distribution, and transfer to nothing.

The notebook already shows four surface signals near chance. That is the experiment, and it came out negative.

replies.body:
> **Priya** · cohort peer

Agreed on the conclusion, but I want to separate two claims because I think only one of them holds.

"Trained on synthetic nulls" is a **data** problem — fixable with real labels, which any real engagement will accumulate anyway.

"Learns surface features rather than entailment" is an **architecture** problem — not fixable by more data of the same kind, because the features on offer genuinely do not contain the signal.

The first is a reason to defer B. The second is a reason to reject it. Worth being clear which one you are asserting, because they imply different roadmaps.

> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

Fair distinction, and I am asserting the second. Score margin, entity-type match and rare-term coverage are all *retrieval confidence* proxies. Sufficiency is a question about whether the evidence **entails** the answer, and entailment is not a monotone function of retrieval confidence — a perfectly retrieved passage can be adjacent to the question and not answer it. No amount of real labels adds a feature that is not there.

comments.body:
> **Marcus** · cohort peer

Is there not a third option nobody has costed? **Run the model call, but not on every query.**

The write-up says "runs on every query in the escalate-by-default design" and then prices Option A against that. But you could gate it: only invoke the sufficiency check when a cheap signal says the query is near the boundary. High retrieval confidence and high margin, skip it. Everything else, pay the 300 ms.

That does not need the classifier to be *correct*. It needs it to be correct on the easy cases, which is a much weaker requirement.

replies.body:
> **Dana** · reviewer · owns the eval harness

This is the right idea and it has a name — a **cascade**, and it is how essentially every production system in this shape actually works. Worth being precise about what it costs, because the trap is subtle.

The requirement is not "correct on easy cases", it is **high precision on the skip decision**. Every query you skip is one where you have decided, without checking, that the evidence is sufficient. A false skip is a confident wrong answer to a handler on a phone call — the exact failure the whole design exists to prevent.

So the cheap gate needs a threshold set for **very high precision on the skip class**, and you accept low recall: skip only when you are extremely confident, pay for everything else. On our data that would mean skipping perhaps the top 20–30% of queries by margin, not 80%.

That still removes a quarter of the cost for a bounded risk, and it is measurable — the abstention machinery in `metrics.abstention_scores` is the right harness. **But notice what happened:** you have reintroduced the classifier from Option B, with a much weaker job. Rafael's objection does not apply, because you are no longer asking it to detect insufficiency, only to detect obvious sufficiency.

comments.body:
Marking this as the answer, because the cascade is the design that comes out of the thread and neither original option is it.

**Decision: Option A, with Marcus's gate, staged.**

**Phase 1 — model call on every query.** Ship the thing that works. Pay the 300 ms and the money. Do not optimise a component whose value you have not yet measured.

**Phase 2 — measure what the check actually catches.** Log every invocation with the retrieval margin. After a few thousand queries you have the joint distribution of margin against the verdict, which is the data the gate needs and which nobody has up front.

**Phase 3 — add the gate, precision-first.** Set the skip threshold for ≥99% precision on the skip class, measured on held-out data. Report the skip rate; expect 20–30%, not 80%. Re-tune on a schedule, because the distribution moves.

**What made Option B wrong as originally posed**, and it is the transferable lesson: it asked a surface-feature classifier to answer an entailment question. Rafael's argument is architectural and no quantity of labels fixes it. **What made the cascade right** is that it asks the same classifier a much easier question — not *"is this evidence sufficient"* but *"is this case obviously easy"* — and that question **is** a monotone function of retrieval confidence.

Reframing a hard question into an easy adjacent one is most of applied ML, and it is worth noticing that it happened here.
